paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Volcanic ash is made of fragments of rock, mineral crystals and volcanic glass that come out of volcanic eruptions. Each piece is less than 2 mm across. People often use the term loosely for everything an explosive eruption throws out, including particles bigger than 2 mm. The correct word for all of that material is tephra.

paragraphs.heading: Bubbles that tear magma apart
paragraphs.text: Explosive eruptions happen when magma decompresses as it rises. Dissolved volatiles, mainly water and carbon dioxide, then come out as gas bubbles. As more bubbles form, the magma turns into a foam. The foam is less dense, and that speeds the magma up the conduit. Fragmentation happens when bubbles fill about 70–80% of the erupting mixture by volume: the violently expanding bubbles tear the magma into fragments, which are thrown into the atmosphere and solidify into ash particles.

paragraphs.heading: When magma meets water
paragraphs.text: Ash also comes from phreatomagmatic eruptions, where magma touches water: the sea, lakes, marshes, groundwater, snow or ice. The magma is much hotter than the boiling point of water, and at first an insulating film of vapour forms between the two. Eventually the film collapses, and cold water and hot magma meet directly. Heat then passes faster, the water expands rapidly, and the magma breaks into small particles that are thrown out of the vent. Breaking up increases the contact area between magma and water, which leads to more fragmentation and fine ash.

paragraphs.heading: Ash made on the move
paragraphs.text: Pyroclastic density currents can produce ash particles as well. Inside these currents particles collide violently and wear each other down, which reduces the grain size and makes fine-grained ash. Large quantities of very fine ash made this way leave the currents in what are called co-ignimbrite ash plumes.

paragraphs.heading: What the chemistry decides
paragraphs.text: The minerals in ash depend on the chemistry of the magma it erupted from. Magma types, and the ash they make, are most often described by their silica content. Low-energy eruptions of basalt give a characteristically dark ash with about 45–55% silica that is generally rich in iron and magnesium. The most explosive rhyolite eruptions give ash with more than 69% silica. Ash of intermediate composition, such as andesite or dacite, has a silica content between 55 and 69%.

paragraphs.heading: Salts, moisture and electricity
paragraphs.text: Sulfate and halide compounds are readily released from fresh volcanic ash. In their solid crystalline form these salts act more as an insulator than a conductor. Once moisture such as fog, mist or light rain dissolves them, the ash may become corrosive and able to conduct electricity. A recent study found that its electrical conductivity goes up with more moisture, more soluble salt and more compaction. This matters a great deal for electric power supply systems.

paragraphs.heading: How far it reaches
paragraphs.text: Once in the air, ash is carried by wind, up to thousands of kilometres away. Because it spreads so widely it can affect society in a number of ways. These include health problems for animals and people, disruption to aviation, disruption to critical infrastructure such as electric power, telecommunications, water networks and transportation, effects on primary industries such as agriculture, and damage to buildings and other structures.
